report:
**Conclusion: generally, no.** For osteoarthritis of the knee, arthroscopy (“keyhole” joint washout, smoothing/debridement, or removal of degenerative meniscal tissue) does **not** provide meaningful, lasting improvement in pain or function compared with non-operative care—and carries surgical risks.

**Why the evidence is persuasive:**

- A pivotal placebo-controlled randomized trial found that lavage and debridement produced outcomes **no better than sham surgery**. This design is particularly important because it controls for the powerful placebo effect of an operation.  
  https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12240635/

- A systematic review/meta-analysis of arthroscopy for degenerative knee disease found, at most, a **small short-term** pain benefit that was not clinically important and did not persist, while harms (though uncommon) occur.  
  https://www.bmj.com/content/350/bmj.h2747

- The BMJ clinical-practice guideline therefore makes a **strong recommendation against** arthroscopy for degenerative knee arthritis/degenerative meniscal tears.  
  https://bjsm.bmj.com/content/52/5/313

- AAOS guidance likewise does not recommend arthroscopic lavage/debridement when symptomatic knee osteoarthritis is the primary diagnosis.  
  https://www.aaos.org/globalassets/quality-and-practice-resources/osteoarthritis-of-the-knee/oak3cpg.pdf

This does not mean arthroscopy is never appropriate: an acute injury or a **true, persistently locked knee** from a displaced fragment may be a different clinical problem. But for pain, stiffness, clicking, or an MRI degenerative meniscal tear in the setting of knee OA, evidence does not support arthroscopy as an effective OA treatment. Exercise/physiotherapy, weight management where relevant, and individualized pain-management options have a stronger role.
